items.title: Climatic Suitability and Invasion Risk of the Elm Zigzag Sawfly in North America
items.abstract: The elm zigzag sawfly, Aproceros leucopoda (Hymenoptera), native to eastern Asia, is among the most concerning potential pests for elm trees (Ulmus spp.); elms form an important component in many North Temperate forests. This sawfly species invaded Europe in 2003 and spread rapidly across much of that continent. In 2020, it was recorded in North America, and it has since become established in several parts of the eastern United States and Canada. Sawfly infestations can cause severe elm tree defoliation, branch die-back that weakens tree health, and potentially tree mortality. Sawfly invasions have the potential to further exacerbate elm decline, especially in conjunction with other pressures, including Dutch elm disease (Ophiostoma ulmi). We used rigorous approaches from distributional ecology to explore climatic suitability for A. leucopoda across North America, considering various sources of uncertainty in the data. We found that, without control, the elm zigzag sawfly could establish populations across eastern Canada and much of the central-eastern and northeastern United States, as well as in the Pacific Northwest. More southern areas of North America were not climatically suitable for this species. Predicted suitable areas for the sawfly overlap broadly with elm distributions, highlighting the need to control this invasion to mitigate potential economic and environmental impacts.

items.title: Coupled MaxEnt-InVEST modelling identifies habitat suitability, quality and conservation gaps of Garrulax maximus
items.abstract: Introduction Habitat degradation and conservation gaps severely threaten China's endemic montane birds, yet few studies have integrated habitat suitability with quality assessment. Methods Using the nationally protected Giant Laughingthrush ( Garrulax maximus ) across five provinces in western China and the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, we coupled optimized MaxEnt, InVEST, and GIS approaches to quantify potential distribution, habitat quality, conservation gaps, and environmental drivers. Results The MaxEnt model performed robustly (mean AUC = 0.946). Climate dominated distribution (69.3% cumulative contribution), with annual precipitation (bio12, 35.7%) as the core limiting factor. The species occupied a cold-humid niche: annual precipitation 631.60–794.65 mm, driest-quarter temperature −7.12–2.75 °C, and elevation 2496.79–4012.78 m. High-suitability areas centered on the western Sichuan Basin rim, decreasing outward. Notably, a spatial mismatch emerged between habitat quality and suitability: Yunnan held the largest high-quality habitat (17.28 × 10 4 km 2 ) but limited priority conservation areas, whereas Sichuan, with less high-quality habitat (13.63 × 10 4 km 2 ), contained the largest priority zones (6.95 × 10 4 km 2 ), indicating complementarity rather than substitution. Conservation gaps were extensive (54.26%–75.98%), mainly along reserve boundaries and buffers, revealing structural deficiencies from overemphasizing core zones while neglecting corridors. Discussion These findings underscore the urgency of reassessing and expanding protected area networks to cover priority zones. Our integrated framework offers a scientific reference for conserving the Giant Laughingthrush and managing montane birds within the Hengduan Mountains biodiversity hotspot, with implications for broader conservation planning in ecologically sensitive regions.

items.title: Current and Future Environmental Suitability of the Nile Grass Rat (Arvicanthis niloticus) in Egypt under CMIP6 Climate Change Scenarios
items.abstract: The Nile grass rat ( Arvicanthis niloticus Desmarest, 1822) is one of the most destructive agricultural rodent pests and a primary reservoir host for multiple zoonotic pathogens in Egypt, including Schistosoma mansoni, Fasciola spp., Hymenolepis nana, murine typhus, and plague (Yersinia pestis via Xenopsylla cheopis fleas). Quantifying how ongoing climate change will alter its potential geographic distribution is essential for national rodent control strategies and vector-borne disease surveillance. In this study, we calibrated an optimized Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt version 3.4.4) ecological niche model to determine the contemporary macroclimatic suitability envelope of A. niloticus across Egypt and projected its potential range shifts for the 2050s (2040–2060) and 2070s (2060–2080) under Phase 6 of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6) Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP2-4.5, moderate-emission; SSP5-8.5, high-emission). The model was calibrated using 31 spatially thinned occurrence records (rarefied with a 10 km buffer) and four non-collinear bioclimatic predictors (VIF < 5): isothermality (Bio 3), minimum temperature of the coldest month (Bio 6), mean temperature of the coldest quarter (Bio 11), and annual precipitation (Bio 12). Hyperparameter tuning using ENMeval identified Linear, Quadratic, and Hinge (LQH) feature classes with a regularization multiplier of 1.0 as the optimal configuration (lowest AICc = 646.68). Across 10-fold bootstrap cross-validation, the model demonstrated high predictive accuracy, yielding a mean training Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) of 0.8623 ± 0.016, a mean test AUC of 0.8513 ± 0.050, and a mean True Skill Statistic (TSS) of 0.543 ± 0.142. Bio 6 emerged as the primary environmental constraint, accounting for 62.6% of the model contribution and 54.6% permutation importance, followed by Bio 11 (26.4% contribution). Using a logistic threshold of 0.245 (10th percentile training presence), approximately 570,489 km² (56.67% of Egypt) is classified within the contemporary macroclimatic suitability envelope, with high suitability concentrated across the Nile Delta, Nile Valley, Fayoum depression, and northern Mediterranean coastal plains. However, realized occupancy is strictly constrained to ~ 4%–5% of the national territory by obligate access to irrigated crops and canal water. Multi-model ensemble consensus projections reveal divergent trajectories: under SSP2-4.5, the climatically suitable envelope expands progressively to 602,952 km² (59.89%) by the 2050s and 596,981 km² (59.30%) by the 2070s under unlimited dispersal assumptions. Conversely, under the extreme SSP5-8.5 scenario, the suitable envelope contracts to 545,686 km² (54.20% of Egypt) by the 2070s—representing a 57.76% contraction of the contemporary range—driven by rising winter minimum temperatures that exceed permissive thermal baselines in Upper Egypt. Crucially, under realistic zero-dispersal constraints across hyper-arid Saharan barriers, the species experiences severe net range contraction without colonizing isolated desert regions. These findings provide vital spatial guidance for proactive rodent management and vector risk containment along current agricultural frontiers and newly reclaimed desert lands.

items.title: Combining ensemble and Bayesian distribution models to guide conservation planning for a narrow‐range endemic skink on ultramafic substrates in New Caledonia
items.abstract: Conservation planning for squamates is frequently constrained by their cryptic ecology and by the rare species conservation paradox, whereby limited distribution data restricts the development of effective management strategies. We focus on Lacertoides pardalis , a narrow endemic skink restricted to ultramafic substrates in New Caledonia, where suitable habitats are increasingly fragmented by nickel mining and recurrent wildfires. To overcome data limitations, we combined ensembles of small models with Bayesian additive regression trees to model habitat suitability using a parsimonious set of bioclimatic variables and a remotely sensed vegetation index (NDVI). We then spatially overlaid predicted suitable habitats with mining concessions, fire history, and protected areas to assess exposure to major anthropogenic pressures. Our results reveal a highly restricted and fragmented potential distribution, with a substantial proportion of suitable habitats overlapping active mining areas and fire‐prone landscapes, while remaining poorly represented within protected areas. By explicitly linking species distribution modeling with spatial threat analysis, this study provides decision‐relevant information to support conservation planning and land‐use management for highly range‐restricted taxa in complex landscapes.

items.title: Environmental suitability for cultivation of sweetleaf, Stevia rebaudiana (Asteraceae, Eupatorieae), in South America: an ensemble species distribution modelling approach using bioclimatic and soil variables
items.abstract: Stevia rebaudiana (Bertoni) Bertoni is a South American crop of increasing agronomic relevance because its leaves accumulate steviol glycosides, high-intensity natural sweeteners used as low-calorie alternatives to sucrose. Although the species is native to Paraguay and adjacent regions, its cultivation has expanded beyond its native range, making the identification of suitable growing areas relevant for agricultural planning under climate change. Here, we modelled the current and future environmental suitability for S. rebaudiana cultivation in South America using cultivation records, bioclimatic variables, and soil predictors. We hypothesized that the main suitability core in southeastern South America would persist under mid-century climate change, with gains and losses concentrated primarily along its margins. A total of 142 georeferenced outdoor cultivation records were compiled from GBIF, iNaturalist, speciesLink, herbarium specimens, and specialized literature. After correlation filtering and exploratory variable selection, 13 predictors were retained, including eight bioclimatic and five edaphic variables. Models were calibrated under current environmental conditions using GLM, MaxEnt, and Random Forest within an ensemble species distribution modelling framework. Because GLM and MaxEnt showed the best balance between AUC and TSS, final current–future projections were based on these algorithms. Future suitability was projected for 2041-2060 under SSP245 and SSP585 using HadGEM3-GC31-LL, GISS-E2-1-G, and MIROC6 climate models combined with present-day soil predictors. Current suitability was highest in Paraguay, northeastern Argentina, Uruguay, and southern to southeastern Brazil. The main predictors were related to seasonal precipitation, annual temperature, and soil conditions. Future projections were consistent with this hypothesis, showing broad persistence of the main suitability core under both SSP245 and SSP585, with gains and losses concentrated mainly in marginal and transitional areas. Suitability gains exceeded losses under both scenarios, resulting in net increases in predicted suitable area of 14.15% and 10.92%, respectively. These results provide a spatial framework for identifying candidate regions for stevia cultivation and for prioritizing field validation under current and future environmental conditions.

items.title: Projecting the potential distribution of sea buckthorn in the Hindu Kush Himalaya under climate change using ensemble species distribution modelling
items.abstract: Sea Buckthorn is a multipurpose shrub valued for its nutrient-rich berries, land aggradation ability, and support to livelihoods in high-altitude regions. However, rapid environmental changes are threatening its habitats. Despite its climatic vulnerability, the impact of climate change on its habitats is poorly understood in the Hindu Kush Himalayas (HKH), a region spanning across eight countries. This critical gap was addressed by a macroecological assessment of the current and projected habitat suitability of H. rhamnoides , H. salicifolia , and H. tibetana across the HKH. Using 864 occurrence records and an ensemble of five algorithms (Artificial Neural Networks, Flexible Discriminant Analysis, Generalized Linear Models, Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines, and Maximum Entropy), our study provides a comprehensive assessment of current and future habitat suitability for H. rhamnoides , H. salicifolia , and H. tibetana . The models performed strongly (AUCroc > 0.94; TSS > 0.76) and showed distinct climatic niches with species-specific responses to future climate change scenarios. H. salicifolia is projected to lose suitable habitat, while H. rhamnoides and H. tibetana are projected to expand under selected climatic scenarios, with the Maximum Temperature of the Warmest Month, emerging as key predictors. Habitat shifts are higher in the Chinese and Indian parts of the HKH. The findings offer important guidance for conservation planning and climate-adaptive management in the Hindu Kush Himalaya. The potential decline of H. salicifolia illustrates the need for targeted monitoring and possible assisted migration, whereas the expansion of the other species presents opportunities for ecological restoration and livelihood enhancement across the fragile HKH.

items.title: Ensemble species distribution modeling and InVEST-based habitat quality assessment for Cupressus funebris under climate change: identifying refugia, ecological security patterns, and conservation priorities in China
items.abstract: Cupressus funebris , an indigenous and ecologically important conifer in China, is increasingly endangered by climate change and habitat fragmentation. Using an ensemble species distribution model (BIOMOD2), we projected current and future habitat suitability under three climate scenarios (SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, SSP5-8.5) for the 2050s, 2070s, and 2090s. We integrated 355 occurrence records and bioclimatic variables using 12 algorithms. We also used the InVEST Habitat Quality model to assess current habitat quality and degradation, and constructed an ecological security pattern from habitat patches and resistance surfaces. This framework identified climate refugia and priority conservation zones. Random Forest performed best (AUC = 0.92 ± 0.02, TSS = 0.85 ± 0.03). Temperature seasonality (Bio04) and minimum temperature of the coldest month (Bio06) were the main climatic drivers. Results show severe range contractions under all scenarios: habitat loss ranges from − 28.5% (SSP1-2.6) to − 62.4% (SSP5-8.5) by the 2090s, with elevational shifts of 180–310 m. Persistent climate refugia (about 15,200 km²) occur in topographically complex regions like the Hengduan Mountains and Northern Yunnan. InVEST showed that high-quality habitat patches are largely restricted to these refugia, while degradation hotspots overlap with projected climate loss zones. A spatial conservation priority map combining climate suitability and habitat quality guides adaptive management, highlighting areas for immediate protection, assisted migration, ex situ conservation, and ecological restoration. This multi-model framework supports climate-resilient conservation strategies for C. funebris .

items.title: Predicted range expansion of Desert Mule Deer under future climate scenarios
items.abstract: The desert mule deer (Odocoileus hemionus crooki) is distributed throughout the southern United States and northern Mexico. As a large herbivore, this subspecies plays a crucial role in maintaining ecological balance. While its distribution is closely linked to water availability and vegetation type, climate change is increasingly altering these factors and shifting potential habitats. This study aimed to model the current potential distribution of O. h. crooki and predict distribution changes for the 2021–2040 period in relation to bioclimatic factors. Presence data were compiled from multiple sources, including GBIF, nocturnal sightings, pellet counts, and camera traps. These records were correlated with 19 bioclimatic variables from WorldClim. We utilized 164 presence points, partitioned into 50% (82 points) for model training and 50% for testing. Ecological niche modeling was performed using the kuenm R package, which provides a robust framework for MaxEnt development. Among the selected variables, BIO 9 (mean temperature of the driest quarter) exhibited the highest contribution to the model, given its high permutation value. Under the future climate scenario of extreme warming (BCC-CSM2-MR model, SSP5-8.5 scenario), the potential distribution of the desert mule deer is predicted to increase by 48.51% in the United States and 45.52% in Mexico. However, actual expansion into these newly suitable areas will likely be constrained by human-dimension factors overlooked by macroclimatic models, including transboundary border infrastructure, urban growth, and novel competitive interactions, emphasizing the need to integrate bioclimatic forecasts with regional land-use and adaptation policies.

items.title: Temperature fluctuations influence predictions of landscape-scale spruce budworm (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae) defoliation in a physiologically informed species distribution model
items.abstract: While many studies on ectotherm thermal tolerance consider temperature exposure, the frequency of temperature exposures is an overlooked driver of survival and fitness that may influence species ranges. We use a physiologically informed species distribution model to evaluate the influence of temperature threshold crossings on defoliation by the spruce budworm, Choristoneura fumiferana (Lepidoptera: Tortricidae), a Canadian boreal forest pest. We combined maps of defoliation between 2006 and 2016 in Quebec with climate, forest, and temperature fluctuation predictors which quantify the number of temperature threshold crossings in a month to train a species distribution model. Our model evaluated how predictors influence spruce budworm defoliation and compared these results to a model trained without temperature fluctuations. Additionally, we investigated the effect of temperature fluctuations on predicted defoliation under 2041–2070 climate change conditions using the models trained with and without temperature fluctuations. We found that the inclusion of temperature fluctuation predictors improved model performance, and these predictors ranked highly in importance relative to other categories. The model trained with temperature fluctuation predictors also predicted vastly different future defoliation patterns across eastern Canada than the model trained without them. Our study reveals the importance of temperature fluctuations on spruce budworm defoliation and demonstrates the influence of physiologically informed predictors in species distribution models.

items.title: Evolution of machine learning-based species distribution models: Technological development, research trends, and future challenges
items.abstract: Species distribution model (SDM) have become important tools for biodiversity assessment, ecological prediction, and conservation planning. Recent advances in machine learning (ML) have expanded their capacity to analyse complex ecological data. However, the overall development trajectory, knowledge structure, and methodological implications of machine learning-based SDM (ML-SDM) remain insufficiently synthesized. This study provides a systematic overview of ML-SDM research from 2006 to 2025 by integrating bibliometric analysis with methodological synthesis. Using 5224 articles retrieved from the Web of Science Core Collection, we combined bibliometric statistics, collaboration analysis, co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, temporal keyword evolution, and qualitative synthesis to investigate research trends, methodological development, knowledge accumulation, and future challenges. The results reveal rapid growth in ML-SDM research and extensive international collaboration, with the United States and China leading in publication output. Early studies established methodological foundations through MaxEnt, Random Forest, and related approaches, followed by increasing attention to model evaluation, sampling bias, and uncertainty assessment. Recent research has increasingly emphasized deep learning (DL), ensemble modelling, remote sensing, and multi-source environmental data. Co-citation and bibliographic coupling analyses further reveal the evolution of methodological knowledge and diversification of modelling approaches. These findings suggest that ML-SDM has undergone a progressive expansion of modelling capability rather than a simple replacement of traditional ML by DL. As a subclass of ML-SDM, DL-SDM extends the capacity to represent complex nonlinear relationships and spatially structured ecological information, while traditional ML remains valuable for many applications. Advances in big data and cloud computing have also supported high-dimensional environmental data integration and scalable ML-SDM applications. However, increasing model complexity and computational capacity do not necessarily improve ecological understanding or predictive reliability. Future ML-SDM research should therefore emphasize the complementary use of traditional ML and DL, together with robust model calibration, ecological interpretability, uncertainty assessment, and spatial transferability.

items.title: Bayesian Wombling for Tracking Invasive Species
items.abstract: This paper develops Bayesian wombling, or boundary analysis for tracking invasive species. We focus on three invasive species of concern in North America: Lycorma delicatula, Adelges tsugae, and Microstegium vimineum. We aim to demonstrate the applicability of wombling for supporting invasive pest management activities. In spatial science wombling is used widely to track regions of rapid change within the spatial reference domain. We use Gaussian process models for point-referenced spatial data followed by predictive inference on rates of change over curves using line integrals. We extend the wombling model based Bayesian inference framework to feature simple analytic forms that avoid high dimensional quadrature while offering uncertainty quantification over curvilinear spatial boundaries.

items.title: AI-Driven Environmental Monitoring for Climate Change and Biodiversity Conservation
items.abstract: Climate change, biodiversity loss, ecosystem degradation, and the increasing frequency of environmental hazards have created an urgent need for intelligent, data-driven environmental monitoring systems. Traditional monitoring approaches often face limitations related to spatial coverage, temporal resolution, data integration, operational cost, and the ability to identify complex environmental patterns. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, geospatial analytics, cloud computing, and big data platforms offer opportunities to improve environmental observation, prediction, and decision-making. This paper examines the role of AI-driven environmental monitoring in climate change assessment and biodiversity conservation, with particular attention to drought prediction, forest fire susceptibility, wetland water-level forecasting, habitat suitability modeling, marine ecosystem monitoring, land-cover classification, and environmental data integration. Existing research indicates that machine learning can support the identification of nonlinear environmental relationships, while remote sensing and geographic information systems can extend monitoring across large and inaccessible regions. IoT sensors and cloud-based infrastructures further enable continuous observation and the integration of heterogeneous environmental datasets. However, the effectiveness of these technologies depends on data quality, model generalizability, computational resources, interpretability, governance, and cooperation among environmental scientists, policymakers, and local communities. This paper develops a conceptual framework connecting environmental data acquisition, data integration, AI-based analysis, risk forecasting, and conservation action. It also discusses implementation challenges, ethical considerations, and future research priorities. The central argument is that AI should complement ecological knowledge and institutional decision-making rather than replace them. Responsible integration of intelligent monitoring systems can strengthen early-warning capabilities, improve conservation planning, and support more adaptive and sustainable environmental management.

items.title: Climate-Based Modeling of Invasive Species Impact on Urban Green Infrastructure Using CLIMEX and Remote Sensing Data
items.abstract: The pace at which invasive alien species are established and spread is becoming a threat, especially to urban ecosystems, due, in part, to the variability of climates, urban growth, and fragmentation of habitats. These biological invasions are highly dangerous to urban green infrastructure (UGI), which sabotages biodiversity, ecological services, and ecological resilience in the long term. A unravelled modelling approach to employ the CLIMEX model of species distribution as well as the spatial analysis of ecosystems via remote sensing to observe invasion risk zones and map them in the fast urbanising landscapes was created in this work. The climatic suitability of chosen invasive species in the current and future climate conditions under parameters serving as temperature, precipitation, and humidity was simulated with the help of the CLIMEX model, and the land cover dynamics and vegetation indices (as well as the urban heat islands) were measured with the assistance of remote sensing data (Sentinel-2 and ModiS) measurements. It was possible to integrate these datasets using a GIS based multi-criteria methodology to create an Invasion Risk Index (IRI) to predict ecologically sensitive regions. The findings indicated that areas with an average rainfall, increasing temperatures, and discontinuous vegetation shows high ecological suitability of the invasive species, and this would be more so at the urban fringes, transport corridors, and industrial areas. These findings underscore the synergistic role of climatic and anthropogenic factors in shaping invasion dynamics and highlight the necessity for adaptive urban planning that incorporates ecological modeling outputs. The proposed framework offers a robust, scalable approach for predicting biological invasions, guiding urban biodiversity conservation strategies, and supporting policymakers in developing climate-resilient, biodiversity-secure urban ecosystems.

items.title: Elodea SDM pipeline: an R workflow for modelling the distribution, nutrient response and spread of Elodea nuttallii and Elodea canadensis in Germany
items.abstract: An R workflow that tests whether an invasive aquatic plant has filled its potential range, and translates the answer into catchment-level management zones. It is applied to Nuttall’s waterweed (Elodea nuttallii), an invasive alien species of Union concern, and its long-established congener Elodea canadensis in Germany. A single script runs every step, from raw GBIF downloads to figures, tables and maps, and writes an audit trail as it goes. The workflow first cleans GBIF records of seven aquatic macrophytes with identical filters (location in Germany, coordinate uncertainty of 10 km or less, collection year 1980 or later, one record per species and location) and thins them spatially. A target-group background built from all surveyed locations corrects for uneven survey effort. Species distribution models (GLM, GAM, GBM and MaxNet in biomod2) are fitted with predictors selected by correlation and variance-inflation screening. They are validated by river-basin cross-validation on ECRINS sub-basins and combined into an ensemble weighted by the true skill statistic. The ensemble is projected to 2021–2040 under CMCC-ESM2 (SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5), with checks for extrapolation, a multivariate environmental similarity surface and response-curve diagnostics. Binomial generalized linear mixed models (lme4) relate occurrence in ECRINS catchments to agricultural phosphorus input and the nitrogen-to-phosphorus input ratio from the Land Use Intensity Index for Stream Ecosystems (LUIS), survey effort and region. A colonisation analysis uses dated records of a single source in Bavaria to model recorded colonisation after an early invasion front, with winter temperature, elevation and straight-line distance to early-invaded catchments as predictors, and downstream position and river-network distance (igraph) in robustness checks. Robustness tests examine sensitivity to data sources (the national atlas, dated records only, records without citizen-science sources and curated sources only), species × region contrasts, block-bootstrap tests of within-region signals, a model trained in the west and projected to the east, alternative regional boundaries, river basin districts and steps in predictors at federal state borders. Further analyses compare the former GDR with eastern Bavaria and test for a step at the former inner-German border, compare winter temperatures with the native range, include catchments recorded only by the study species in the colonisation analysis, check residual spatial autocorrelation and alternative suitability thresholds, and summarise all key odds ratios in one robustness figure. Finally, each ECRINS catchment is assigned to a management zone, from harvest candidate to prevention priority, based on its records, river basin district and predicted suitability. Fitted models are stamped with their settings and inputs and reused only when the stamp matches, and a preflight check lists all missing inputs before any long computation starts. Input data are not redistributed. They are available from GBIF (https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.dhvq4g and https://doi.org/10.15468/dl.x4fhp2), WorldClim v2.1, LUIS 2017 (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17204506), EEA ECRINS v1.1 and GADM v4.1. README.md gives the expected folder layout, requirements, run instructions and the mapping of the article’s figures and tables to the outputs; CHANGELOG.md lists the changes between versions. The workflow was tested with R 4.5.2, terra 1.9-1, biomod2 4.3-4-5, mgcv 1.9-3, gbm 2.2.3, maxnet 0.1.4, caret 7.0-1 and lme4 1.1-38.

items.title: Prioritizing spatial extent over resolution in shaping the performance of species distribution models: Insights from a multi-scale assessment of Cerris oaks in China
items.abstract: Species distribution models (SDMs) are essential tools for predicting the impacts of climate change on biodiversity. However, their predictive performance remains strongly scale-dependent, posing a persistent challenge in biogeography. Particularly, the combined effects of spatial extent and resolution on model transferability and ecological interpretability remain poorly understood. Here, we developed a multi-scale assessment framework that integrates three spatial extents (national, subtropical, and warm-temperate) with five spatial resolutions (1, 2, 4, 8, and 16 km) to evaluate SDMs performance across scales. Using three sympatric Cerris oaks in China (Quercus acutissima, Quercus variabilis, and Quercus chenii), we employed ensemble models validated with prevalence-independent Sørensen’s similarity metrics, overprediction rate, and underprediction rate to assess scale-dependent variations in model accuracy and predictive outcomes; identify scale-sensitive environmental predictors; and quantify the effects of spatial scaling on ecological response curves. Our results indicate that spatial extent was the most influential factor affecting the SDMs predictive accuracy. Q. chenii—benefiting from more complete spatial coverage—experienced less niche truncation and achieved higher accuracy across scales than the more widespread Q. acutissima and Q. variabilis. Regardless of resolution, national-scale models also consistently outperformed climatic-zone models, which exhibited a higher risk of underprediction. Notably, increasing spatial resolution did not necessarily improve model accuracy. Additionally, key environmental drivers were consistent across spatial resolutions but varied substantially among spatial extents. This study highlights the critical influence of spatial scale, recommending that researchers prioritize using a species’ full geographic range to avoid spatial truncation before selecting a resolution suited to its ecological niche.

items.title: Habitat Suitability of Mango Bacterial Black Spot Disease Under Different Climate Scenarios Using MaxEnt
items.abstract: Intensified globalisation and the movement of plant materials have increased pathways for plant invasions and the risk of plant disease establishment globally. Mango bacterial black spot (MBBS) is an invasive disease native to Africa. The disease poses a serious threat to global mango production and trade. Yet MBBS habitat‐suitability models that can guide surveillance and monitoring programmes remain poorly documented. This study predicts global climate‐suitable areas for MBBS using the Maximum Entropy model. Future projections were conducted under two socioeconomic pathways (SSPs245 and 585) and two time periods (2050s: 2041–2060 and 2070s: 2061–2080). The models showed strong predictive performance (AUC = 0.890, TSS = 0.686, and CBI = 0.705). Among the bioclimatic variables, the minimum temperature of the coldest month, the mean temperature of the warmest quarter, precipitation of the wettest month and the precipitation seasonality contributed the most to the model. Under current conditions, parts of South America, Africa, Asia and Australia were found to be suitable. These areas will become more suitable for disease establishment in the future. Areas suitable for MBBS establishment are projected to increase by 1.60% and 2.01% under SSP245 and SSP585, respectively, in the 2050s. Similarly, in the 2070s, suitability gains are projected at 1.91% and 2.78% under SSP245 and SSP585, respectively. These findings provide insight into the habitat suitability of the MBBS disease and are useful for surveillance and monitoring programs.

items.title: Global Potential Distribution and Climatic Niche Dynamics of the Invasive Alien Weed Solanum rostratum Dunal
items.abstract: Whether invasive species conserve their ancestral climatic niches or undergo realized niche changes during global spread fundamentally affects the reliability of invasion risk projections. We integrated ensemble species distribution models (SDMs), the extended COUE framework, and Multivariate Environmental Similarity Surfaces (MESS) to quantify the global climatic niche dynamics and invasion risk of Solanum rostratum Dunal (Solanaceae) across its native North America and four invaded regions. Macroecological modeling revealed a temperature-driven, precipitation-constrained distribution, where thermal availability and mean diurnal range dictated suitability, while precipitation extremes imposed strict limits. Cross-regional analyses comparing true occurrence records revealed a highly heterogeneous continuum of realized niche dynamics. Populations in Australia and Russia-Eastern Europe exhibited strict climatic conservatism, occupying analogous climates with complete niche stability (S = 1.000). Western European populations displayed substantial niche unfilling (U = 0.321); however, 80.4% of this constituted abandonment (native climates absent from Europe), suggesting genuine dispersal limitation. In contrast, Chinese populations exhibited extensive colonization of novel climatic conditions. Although showing near-complete stability strictly within available analogous climates (S = 0.998), 48.5% of the expansion-related niche quantity in China occurred in non-analog environments (pioneering), leading to poor projection transferability of the native SDM (Continuous Boyce Index = 0.166). These findings demonstrate that S. rostratum maintains ancestral climatic preferences where suitable environments are available while possessing the capacity to pioneer novel climatic spaces during global invasion. Integrating these expanded realized tolerances into a global ensemble SDM provides a robust, region-specific risk assessment framework that improves projection accuracy and supports adaptive management under global environmental change.

items.title: Climatic Niche‐Based Identification of In‐Situ Climate Refugia to Support China's Conservation Planning Toward the 30 × 30 Target
items.abstract: Aim Climate change increasingly threatens biodiversity by altering habitat conditions and undermining the long‐term effectiveness of protected area (PA) networks. In situ climate refugia—locations that retain relatively stable climatic conditions—are essential for supporting species persistence under future climate scenarios and for meeting global conservation targets such as “30 × 30.” This study aims to identify in situ climate refugia across China using a climatic niche–based framework and to assess the degree to which these refugia are represented within the existing PA network. Location Mainland China. Time Period Baseline (1970–2000) and future projections for 2081–2100 under SSP2‐4.5 and SSP5‐8.5 scenarios Major Taxa Studied 282 endangered terrestrial vertebrates, including 68 mammals, 153 amphibians, 35 reptiles, and 26 non‐migratory birds. Methods We developed a climatic niche–based framework that integrates species‐specific climatic tolerances, climate change intensity, and habitat suitability to identify potential climate refugia at a national scale. Unlike traditional approaches reliant on broad, species‐neutral climate stability thresholds, our method uses species‐specific climatic niche widths (CNWs) to derive ecologically grounded climatic tolerance thresholds, enabling more species‐informed identification of refugial areas. Results Approximately 23% of mainland China's land area was classified as high‐potential climate refugia, concentrated mainly in the subtropical evergreen broadleaf forest and tropical monsoon rainforest. However, only 15% of these areas currently fall within PAs. Incorporating high‐potential refugia alone could increase national PA coverage from 19% to 38%, while adding medium‐potential refugia could raise overall protection to 56%. Main Conclusions Species‐specific CNWs provide a realistic and ecologically informed basis for delimiting refugia under climate change. The pronounced mismatch between identified climate refugia and China's existing PA network highlights critical conservation gaps, especially within subtropical and tropical biomes. High‐ and medium‐potential refugia identify opportunities for further ecological assessment and protection planning toward the 30 × 30 target. The proposed framework is scalable and applicable to other regions seeking to incorporate climate‐adaptive principles into systematic conservation planning.

items.title: Relationship Between Predicted Habitat Suitability and Population Density of Game Mammals Under a Sharply Continental Climate
items.abstract: This study evaluates the relationship between MaxEnt-predicted habitat suitability and departmental estimates of population density for 14 game mammal species in the Pavlodar Region. Model performance varied substantially among species (Test AUC = 0.538-0.992; TSS = 0.220-0.984), and extremely high AUC values for some species with small samples were interpreted cautiously. For 41 territorial units, habitat suitability was aggregated as the mean MaxEnt value within each polygon and compared with density using Spearman's rank correlation. Spearman's r s ranged from 0.288 to 0.738; in the initial analysis, a statistically significant positive relationship was detected for 13 of the 14 species, whereas the relationship was not statistically significant for the steppe polecat (r s = 0.288; p = 0.068). Residual spatial autocorrelation assessed with Moran's I was non-significant for 11 species; for wolf, bobak marmot, and roe deer, an additional spatially constrained permutation analysis was performed. After this analysis, the relationship remained significant for wolf (r s = 0.714, p = 0.0007) and roe deer (r s = 0.488, p = 0.0198), whereas for bobak marmot it remained positive but was not statistically significant after accounting for spatial structure (r s = 0.467; p = 0.0615). The results indicate that habitat suitability reflects the environmental potential of an area but is not a direct measure of population density.
